1.summary: A multipurpose server is a non-dedicated server that performs multiple functions, for example a file server and a print server at the same time.
1.deeper: Non-dedicated (multi-function) servers provide multiple network services and local access for users. A non-dedicated server is expected to be more flexible in its day-to-day use than a dedicated server. It can direct network traffic and perform administrative actions, and it is often used as a front end for the administrator to work with other applications or services, or to perform services for more than one network. A non-dedicated web server serves out websites but might also function as a print server on the local network, or as the administrator's workstation. In a small network, many services can be handled by one multipurpose, non-dedicated server. In a medium to large network, there can be many dedicated servers, each performing separate tasks. Most networks use a combination of both types: multipurpose for flexibility, single-purpose for efficiency and performance.
1.analogy: A multipurpose server is like a pocket knife with several tools: one item covers many small jobs. A workshop with a separate tool for each job is better for heavy work.
1.scenario: A small office network needs file sharing, printing and a website. An airman handles all of these services with one multipurpose server. A large wing network, by contrast, uses many dedicated servers, each performing a separate task.
1.example: A family car carries people, groceries and luggage; it is flexible rather than built for one job. In the course: A multipurpose server can be, for example, both a file server and a print server at the same time, Block Text p.3.

1.summary: A dedicated server is a single-function server assigned to provide specific applications or services for the network and nothing else.
1.deeper: A dedicated (single-purpose) server is committed to a specific task. End users don't sit at these machines to do their daily work. Because it specializes in only a few tasks, it requires fewer resources than a non-dedicated server might, and the savings may translate to efficiency and better network performance. A web server is an example: it serves up web pages and nothing else. A print server is another: it facilitates printing and nothing else. A non-dedicated (multipurpose) server is the other side: it performs multiple functions and is more flexible. Many networks use both, gaining performance from the dedicated servers and flexibility from the non-dedicated ones. The word "dedicated" also names the client-server model (the dedicated model); a dedicated server is one server with a single function.
1.analogy: A dedicated server is like a cook who only makes coffee: one job, done quickly, with little equipment. A cook who also bakes and serves tables is more flexible but slower at each job.
1.scenario: An airman compares two servers. One only serves out websites, and nobody sits at it to work. The other serves websites, acts as a print server on the local network and is also the administrator's workstation. The first is a dedicated server; the second is non-dedicated.
1.example: A ticket machine that only sells tickets does one thing and does it fast. In the course: A dedicated server is assigned to provide specific applications or services for the network and nothing else, Block Text p.4.

1.summary: Peer-to-peer is the decentralized, non-dedicated network model: there are no dedicated servers, and every computer can communicate directly with every other computer.
1.deeper: Peer-to-peer networking is one of the simplest ways to configure a network and spread network resources among all clients. There are no dedicated servers, and every computer can communicate directly with every other computer. By default, no computer has more authority than any other, though each computer can be configured to share only some of its resources and keep others inaccessible. Management is decentralized, so every device can function as either a server or a client on an as-needed basis. Most peer-to-peer implementations aren't robust enough to support large traffic spikes. Workgroups are commonly known as peer-to-peer networks: there is no centralized control, no formal membership and no network authentication, and computers act as standalone systems. While a computer shares its files, it acts as a server and controls access to them; when it requests data from another computer, it acts as a client and the other computer is the server.
1.analogy: Peer-to-peer is like a group of neighbors lending tools to each other: there is no tool shop, anyone can lend or borrow, and whoever lends a tool decides who gets it.
1.scenario: Four computers in a small workgroup are linked to each other with no server. One computer shares a folder; another requests a file from it. While it shares, the first computer acts as the server and controls access to its folder; the requesting computer acts as the client.
1.example: Friends at a table who pass dishes directly to each other need no waiter. In the course: Peer-to-peer networking is one of the simplest ways to configure a network and spread network resources among all clients in a network, Block Text p.5.

1.summary: Client-server is the dedicated, centralized network model: each computer is configured either as a client or a server, and clients use the server as an intermediary.
1.deeper: In client-server architecture, each computer is configured either as a client or a server. Clients send a request or query to the server and the server responds; clients do not share their resources directly with each other but use the server as an intermediary. It is also called the dedicated model, and it is centralized. A domain is commonly known as a client/server network: the network is controlled from a single, centralized point, and the server controls the access of the clients through network authentication. Its advantages are central management of the server, security (administrators define rules for security and access rights as requests are monitored and logged), and easier organization and management of resources, including backups from a centralized data source. Its disadvantages: servers are more expensive to set up and maintain; adding clients increases the workload on the server and the bandwidth used on the network, since all client requests go through the server; and it is extremely reliant on the centralized server. Should the server fail, the network could collapse, the clients cannot function until it is restored, and if it held the only copy of the data, all the data could be lost if there is no backup.
1.analogy: Client-server works like a library with one front desk: readers do not hand books to each other but ask the desk, which keeps the records and decides who may borrow. If the desk closes, nobody can borrow anything.
1.scenario: Network administrators plan a new network and want a centralized administrative environment, so they set it up as a domain: a client/server network. Each computer is a client or a server, and the server controls everyone's access through network authentication. They also plan a backup, because the network relies on that one server.
1.example: In a company where every order goes through one central office, nothing is sent directly from desk to desk. In the course: Client-server architecture is a network where each computer is configured either as a client or a server, Block Text p.5.

1.summary: A server is a computer or device on the network that manages shared resources for other systems; it serves resources up to network users.
1.deeper:
Servers are a core component of the network, providing the resources users need to perform tasks. A server usually has more processing power, memory and hard disk space than clients, and runs network operating software to manage not only data but also users, groups, security and applications. Servers can centralize the control of resources and security, distribute processes to balance the load on computers, and compartmentalize files, so if one server goes down, not all the files are lost. Any device providing resources on a network is behaving as a server. Many types exist, such as file servers and print servers; a small network may use one multipurpose server, while a medium to large network usually has multiple single-purpose servers.

Active Directory Server: also known as a domain controller. Its role in Active Directory lets administrators manage and store information about network resources, and application data, in a distributed database (Unit 3).

Application Server: referred to as a type of middleware, software that provides services to applications beyond those available from the operating system. It sits between database servers and the end user and often connects the two.

Domain Name System (DNS) Server: provides a translation, or resolution, of domain names to IP addresses. A computer does not understand where the human-readable www.cnn.com is; DNS finds its machine-readable IP address. It translates host names to IP addresses and vice versa (Unit 4).

Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Server: automatically assigns each computer an Internet Protocol (IP) address from a list of available addresses, which reduces configuration time (Unit 5).
1.analogy: A server is like the supply room of a unit: it holds what everyone shares and hands it out on request. Different supply rooms specialize: one keeps the roster, one hands out address cards, one answers where things are.
1.scenario: A new computer joins the network. The DHCP server assigns it an IP address from its list. When its user types a web address, the DNS server translates the name into an IP address. The user then signs in, and the Active Directory server holds the information about that user and the network's resources.
1.example: A restaurant kitchen serves every table from one place, so the tables do not cook for themselves. In the course: A server is a computer or device on the network managing shared resources for other systems on the network, Block Text p.5.

1.summary: A client is a computing device that initiates contact with a server to make use of a shareable resource.
1.deeper: On a client-server network, clients send a request or query to the server and the server responds accordingly. Clients may still run applications from, and save data to, their local hard disk, but by connecting to a server they can also use shared applications, data and devices. Clients do not share their resources directly with each other; they use the server as an intermediary. There are two types of clients: the thin client and the thick client. In some cases a client could also act as a server, because the term "client" also describes the role a device is performing. The word may also refer to the human user of a client workstation, or to the client software installed on it.
1.analogy: A client is like a customer at a counter: the customer walks up, asks for something, and the clerk behind the counter answers. The customer starts the exchange; the counter serves.
1.scenario: An airman's laptop needs a shared file. The laptop contacts the server and sends a request; the server responds, and the laptop uses the file. In that exchange the laptop is the client. Later the same laptop works on a document saved on its own local hard disk without asking the server for anything.
1.example: A diner who orders a meal starts the exchange, and the kitchen answers the order. In the course: A client is a computing device that initiates contact with a server to make use of a shareable resource, Block Text p.6.

1.summary: A thin client is a software program or computer that relies heavily on another computer, the network server, to do most of its work.
1.deeper: A thin client is a desktop terminal with a small or no SSD/HDD. It operates as part of a network, with the client software or computer acting as an interface and the network server doing all the real work. All features typically found on a desktop PC, such as applications and memory, are stored on the server back at the data center; the thin client relies on that central server for applications, processing and memory. Thin clients can be found in medical offices, airline ticketing kiosks, schools, governments, manufacturing plants and call centers. Along with being easy to install, they offer a lower total cost of ownership (TCO) than thick clients. A thick client, by contrast, has many applications installed locally and can run on its own.
1.analogy: A thin client is like a TV remote: it has buttons and sends your choices, but the picture is made somewhere else.
1.scenario: At an airline ticketing kiosk, a customer types at a terminal that has no hard drive. The terminal is only the interface; the applications and memory are on the server at the data center, which does the real work. The kiosk is a thin client.
1.example: A phone call to a help line puts your questions to a person who does the looking up for you. In the course: The term thin client refers to either a software program or actual computer relying heavily on another computer to do most of its work, Block Text p.6.

1.summary: A thick client, also known as a fat or rich client, is a workstation in a client-server configuration that functions independently of the server.
1.deeper: A thick client has a CPU, memory, an SSD/HDD and local applications: many applications are installed locally on the client hard drive. It pulls some data from the central server but only occasionally needs to be connected to that server; it can run on its own without always being connected. It still depends on the central server for some data, but can function independently. The thin client is the other type of client: a desktop terminal with a small or no SSD/HDD that relies on the central server for applications, processing and memory. Thin clients offer a lower total cost of ownership (TCO) than thick clients.
1.analogy: A thick client is like a soldier with a full pack: food, tools and supplies are carried along, so the soldier can work for a long time away from base and only checks in now and then.
1.scenario: An airman's laptop has its applications installed on its own hard drive. It connects to the central server once in a while to pull some data, then works on its own. The laptop is a thick client.

1.summary: A workstation is a personal computer, such as a desktop or laptop, with all the essential hardware and software to function without a network.
1.deeper: A workstation has all its components: CPU, memory, SSD/HDD. It may or may not be connected to a network, and it can function completely independently of a server or network, though few users would find much use for an offline device. Most clients on a military network are workstation computers. A workstation is one of the components of client-server architecture, together with the server, the thin client and the thick client. 1.summary: A Telnet server lets users remotely log on to a host computer and execute tasks, using its programs and data as if they were on the local machine; it is not secure.

1.summary: A virtual server re-creates the functionality of a physical server by converting one physical server into multiple virtual machines (VMs) that users share.
1.deeper: Virtualizing servers involves converting one physical server into multiple virtual machines (VMs). A virtual server virtually re-creates the functionality of a physical server, which makes it easy to reallocate resources and adapt to dynamic workloads. It supports multiple owners: each owner uses and administers the system's services as if they had complete control of the server, and a device may not realize there is another virtual machine running on the virtual server. A virtual server is configured so that multiple users can share its processing power, and it is often located in an off-site data center or a cloud environment.
1.analogy: A virtual server is like one building divided into apartments: each tenant has their own front door and runs their own home as if it were a whole house, while all of them share one building.
1.scenario: One physical server in an off-site data center is converted into three virtual machines. Three owners each administer one VM as if they had complete control of the server, and none of them needs to know the others' VMs are there. When one owner's workload grows, resources are reallocated.
1.example: Office workers who share one big printer each send their own jobs as if the printer were theirs alone. In the course: Virtualizing servers involves converting one physical server into multiple virtual machines (VMs), Block Text p.10.

2.summary: Virtualization simply separates hardware from software, so multiple software products can share a single hardware resource, each operating as though it has complete control of it.
2.deeper:
A virtual machine (VM) is a combination of software applications and an operating system tricked into thinking it has its own dedicated hardware, while that hardware may be shared with several other VMs. Many VMs can run on one piece of hardware, which gives a much better utilization rate of server hardware while still isolating applications. That saves on hardware and its maintenance contracts, and on the electricity needed to run and cool it in the data center.

Virtualization has three primary components: the host server, the hypervisor or Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM), and the guest operating system. Organizations turn to it as a cost-effective way to reach their goals: it improves server utilization, streamlines management, saves time and money, and gives better continuity of the IT environment.
2.analogy: Virtualization is like an apartment building. One building stands on one foundation, but each household lives behind its own door as if the place were all its own.
2.scenario: An airman's unit has one powerful server. Instead of buying a machine for each software product, the unit separates the software from that hardware: several products now run on the one server, each acting as though it controls the hardware alone.
2.example: Four pots can cook on one stove at once, each on its own burner, and none of them needs a stove of its own. Virtualization lets software share hardware in the same way. In the course: Virtualization simply separates hardware from software, Block Text p.11.

2.summary: A virtual machine (VM) is a combination of software applications and an operating system tricked into thinking it has its own dedicated hardware.

2.summary: The host server is the computer on which the virtualized environment resides: the hardware that provides processing power, memory, disk and network input/output.
2.deeper:
The host server may have its own operating system installed. Host server hardware is the computer components running all server operations; they do the work. Hardware requirements depend on the number and roles of the virtual machines the host will manage, so it is almost impossible to recommend one set. Like any computing device, the host needs a CPU, RAM, storage, multiple NICs and I/O device support. Processing power and memory are the main factors limiting the number of VMs a host can support; a shortage in either directly affects the performance of all VMs, so a CPU optimized for virtualization is best. Storage must have the proper space allotted to run the number of VMs needed, and speed-sensitive systems use solid state disks (SSD) instead of hard disk drives (HDD).

Network Interface Card: the number of NICs varies with the tasks of the VMs on the host. A host server can operate with two, but no less than four is recommended for optimal network bandwidth, redundancy and speed, or to separate traffic to different networks.

Input/Output (I/O) Device Support: the host server needs a means to interact with the user to make software and system configurations. Input/output devices such as a mouse, keyboard and monitor do this; almost all servers now use USB for them.

Graphics Processing Unit: most host servers have an on-board graphics processing unit (GPU) so a monitor can be connected. A host server without an integrated GPU needs an adapter card installed on the motherboard.
2.analogy: A host server is like the engine room of a ship. The passengers never see it, but every cabin's light and heat comes from the machinery down there.
2.scenario: An airman checks a new host server before VMs are added. It has a CPU and RAM to run them, storage for their files, several NICs for network traffic, and a keyboard, mouse and monitor plugged in so the airman can make software and system configurations.
2.example: A power strip feeds several lamps from one wall outlet; each lamp works only because the outlet supplies it. The host server supplies its VMs in the same way. In the course: The host server is the computer on which the virtualized environment resides, Block Text p.12.

2.summary: Desktop virtualization is a method of simulating a user workstation so it can be accessed from a remotely connected device.
2.deeper: It separates the desktop computer environment from the physical device used to access it, and it is often used to move workloads into isolated environments to reduce system administration requirements. Its three primary architectures can overlap. Presentation virtualization delivers desktops or applications from a shared server: users share a presentation session, and the client sees only a picture of the application, with no processing on the client; applications are installed only once for all the users who share them. Virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) creates simulated desktops on a 1:1 relationship, one VM for one client, so users do not share the environment. User profile virtualization decouples a user's profile, settings and data from the operating system and stores them in a centralized data share; it gives a follow-me identity, so a worker reaches the same workspace without being tied to a single device or location.
2.analogy: Desktop virtualization is like a locker you can open from any door of a building: your things live in one place, and you reach them from wherever you walk in.
2.scenario: An airman logs in from a borrowed laptop and sees the same workstation as at the office. The workstation is simulated on a server and reached from a remotely connected device; which architecture serves it depends on whether users share a server, get one VM each, or carry their profile from device to device.
2.example: A streamed film plays on whatever screen is at hand, while the film itself is kept elsewhere. A virtual desktop reaches the user the same way. 2.summary: Virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) is a desktop virtualization architecture that creates simulated desktops for clients on a 1:1 relationship: one VM for one client, so users do not share the environment.
2.deeper:
In simplest terms, a VDI can be a simulated or virtual desktop computer. Since each client is totally separate from the others on the server, VDI allows for flexibility, management and security.

Presentation virtualization is the contrast: it delivers desktops or applications from a shared server, users share the presentation session, and the client sees only a picture of the application.
2.analogy: VDI is like issuing each member of a team a personal locker instead of one shared shelf: nobody's things mix with anyone else's.
2.scenario: Each airman in a training section logs in to a VDI desktop. Every airman has a VM of their own, and nobody shares an environment. Since each client is totally separate on the server, the section gets flexibility, management and security.
2.example: Hotel guests each get a room of their own instead of sharing one. A VDI desktop is one per user in the same way. In the course: Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) creates simulated desktops for clients on a 1:1 relationship (1 VM for 1 client), Unit 2a–b Slides p.15.

2.summary: Server virtualization, the most common type of virtualization, partitions a physical server (the host) into smaller virtual servers that interact with other servers, applications and client devices just as physical servers would.
2.deeper:
The partitioning hides the server's hardware resources from users, including the number and identity of individual host servers, processors and operating systems. Virtualizing servers separates the operating system and its applications from the physical hardware underneath. The intention is to spare the user from understanding and managing complicated details of server resources, while increasing resource sharing and utilization and keeping the capacity to expand later. It is done with software like VMware, Citrix XenServer or Microsoft Hyper-V. Its three architectures are operating-system-level virtualization, hardware emulation and paravirtualization.

VMware: server virtualization software named as the current industry leader. Its ESXi is a Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor, while VMware Workstation and VMware Fusion are hosted (Type 2) hypervisors.

Microsoft Hyper-V: server virtualization software from Microsoft, and also an example of a bare-metal (Type 1) hypervisor.

Paravirtualization: a technique that allows the guest OS running in a virtual machine to have some access and control to the underlying server hardware. It increases software processing by streamlining communication.
2.analogy: Server virtualization is like dividing one large hall into offices with movable walls. Visitors see separate offices with their own doors; the building behind the walls stays out of their sight.
2.scenario: An airman's unit runs one physical host partitioned into several virtual servers with VMware. Client devices and other servers talk to each virtual server just as they would to a physical one, and nobody using them sees the host's processors or operating systems.
2.example: One large house can be split into several apartments, each with its own door and address, and visitors treat each as a separate home. Server virtualization splits a server the same way. In the course: Server virtualization is the partitioning of a physical server into smaller virtual servers, Block Text p.14.

2.summary: Hardware emulation is a server virtualization architecture in which the host or hypervisor emulates a certain piece of hardware and presents it to the guest virtual server, regardless of what physical hardware is installed.
2.deeper: The host's physical hardware can be completely different from what it emulates. An example is emulating another network device, like a switch or router, on a server instead of purchasing and installing a physical one. That saves the maintenance and administration costs of the physical switch or router, its power and the rest. It works like a videogame emulator, which mimics hardware to run software. Hardware emulation is one of the three server virtualization architectures, with operating-system-level virtualization and paravirtualization.
2.analogy: Hardware emulation is like a flight simulator: the trainee works real-looking controls, though no aircraft is there, and the simulator answers just as the aircraft would.
2.scenario: A virtual server needs a switch. Instead of purchasing and installing a physical switch, the airman has the host emulate one and present it to the guest virtual server. The host's own hardware is nothing like a switch, but the guest uses the emulated switch all the same.
2.example: A games console emulator lets old games run on a computer that is nothing like the old console. 2.summary: Application virtualization runs specific software applications on central servers, separated from the underlying hardware end users access, so multiple users can use the same installed application at once.
2.deeper:
Instead of the one-to-one relationship of a standard desktop, the applications are centrally installed and managed and then "served up" to the end user's remote device, which simplifies their installation, configuration and lifecycle management. It has two kinds.

Application virtualization lets applications run in environments that are foreign to them. A common software baseline across many computers reduces system integration and administration costs, and operating system migrations get simpler: applications move to removable media or between computers without being installed, becoming portable software. It is particularly useful for older industrial software that only runs on legacy operating systems: the new OS keeps its up-to-date security patches and the old software still works.

Application streaming is an on-demand delivery model. Most applications need only a small portion of their code to operate, so the program need not be fully installed on the client; portions are offered across the network when required. Like a progressive download of audio or video, it is totally transparent to the end user, and it is commonly used with desktop virtualization.
2.analogy: Application virtualization is like a library reading room: one copy of a reference book sits on the central shelf, and many readers use it without each buying their own.
2.scenario: A squadron depends on an old program that only runs on a legacy operating system, but every workstation must keep its new, patched system. The program is virtualized and served from a central server, so airmen use it while their own systems stay current.
2.example: A streaming music service plays a song while it is still arriving, with nothing to install first. Application streaming works the same way. In the course: Application virtualization is running specific software applications on central servers while separating these applications from the underlying hardware the end users are accessing, Block Text p.16.

2.summary: Server consolidation is perhaps the easiest, most obvious application of virtualization: it increases the utilization of existing resources, so fewer physical servers must be maintained and costs drop.
2.deeper: It addresses the financial problems many organizations face. After consolidation, administrators can optimize server resources for use by other VMs, and the cost of maintaining the servers the organization had before goes down. As a benefit of virtualization it simplifies infrastructure: consolidating servers using VMs reduces the number of physical servers required to meet operational needs, letting one server host many once-dedicated servers that may have been underutilized in their stand-alone state. Administrators then manage less overall infrastructure: devices, racks, cables and power. One physical host can be home to a virtual domain controller, DHCP server and DNS server, each still with a single function but using the host's shared resources. Consolidation also lowers the total cost of ownership, addresses environmental issues and improves responsiveness.
2.analogy: Server consolidation is like moving several half-empty offices into one well-used floor: fewer rooms to heat, clean and pay for, and each team still has its own desk.
2.scenario: A wing finds that its domain controller, DHCP server and DNS server each run on a machine of their own, mostly idle. They are consolidated as VMs onto one host server; each keeps its single function, and the wing maintains far fewer physical servers.
2.example: Several family members who each drive a nearly empty car to the same place can share one car instead. In the course: Server consolidation is perhaps the easiest, most obvious application of virtualization, Block Text p.18.

2.summary: Load balancing involves running two or more VMs on separate pieces of hardware and dividing the regular workload between them.
2.deeper: It protects against single point of failure issues: with VMs on separate pieces of hardware, the loss of one machine will not hinder operations. It also makes better use of machine resources: rather than some VMs sitting idly, all VMs carry a portion of the load, and idle virtual machines are recruited to assist with loads, so resources are not going unused. Load balancing is also a benefit of virtualization because it lets VMs dynamically adjust to the demands of applications and improve responsiveness. A load balancer can even spin up new VMs on the fly, which is one reason asset tracking matters in a virtual environment.
2.analogy: Load balancing is like two cooks sharing the orders in a kitchen. Neither stands idle, and if one has to step away, the other keeps the orders going.
2.scenario: A unit runs its service on VMs on two separate servers, with the regular workload divided between them. One server fails; the VMs on the other server carry the load, and users notice nothing.
2.example: Two checkout lanes open at a store share the line of shoppers, and if one register breaks, the other keeps serving. In the course: Load balancing involves running two or more VMs on separate pieces of hardware and dividing the regular workload between them, Block Text p.18.

2.summary: Server pooling uses virtualization software to manage a group, or pool, of virtualized servers; the software picks the physical server best suited to run each machine.
2.deeper: Instead of installing a virtual machine on a particular server, administrators merely point the virtualization software at the virtual machine image, and the software figures out which physical server is best suited to run the machine. Software-enabled pooling streamlines administration, management and performance: administrators don't need to look for optimal servers. It is useful for large organizations with many devices.
2.analogy: Server pooling is like a taxi dispatcher: the rider names where to go, and the dispatcher picks whichever car is best placed, so the rider never hunts for one.
2.scenario: An administrator in a large organization has a new VM to run. Rather than checking each host for room, the administrator points the virtualization software at the VM image, and the software places it on the physical server best suited to it.
2.example: A restaurant host seats each party at the best open table, so guests never search the room themselves. In the course: Server pooling utilizes virtualization software to manage a group, or pool, of virtualized servers, Block Text p.18.

2.summary: Disaster recovery (DR) refers to products and processes helping organizations respond to catastrophic situations: incidents far worse than a single virtual machine crashing or a piece of hardware failing.
2.deeper: DR comes into play within medium to large organizations that manage network systems and data centers, for example when an entire data center is temporarily or permanently lost. It is critical for organizations to have a DR plan. Virtualization is an ideal technology for disaster recovery because VM images can be captured in files and then be started by the hypervisor; VM files and snapshots can be easily reloaded. Virtualization saves all data in a file format, and snapshots allow restoration of a machine to an earlier system state.
2.analogy: A DR plan is like a fire evacuation plan for a building: nobody uses it for a burnt slice of toast, but when the whole building is at risk, everyone follows it.
2.scenario: One VM on a host crashes; that alone is not a disaster. Months later a storm takes a whole data center offline. Now the organization follows its DR plan, and the hypervisor starts the VM images captured in files.
2.example: A family keeps copies of its important papers somewhere else, ready in case the house is lost. In the course: Disaster Recovery (DR) refers to products and processes helping organizations respond to catastrophic situations, Block Text p.18.

2.summary: Availability is the security fundamental of ensuring that all data will be readily available to those with appropriate authorization.
2.deeper: In a virtual environment, changes to the base infrastructure can affect the fundamentals of security, availability among them; integrity, another, means ensuring that data remains uncompromised. Making a change at the base level is like upgrading the hardware or firmware on a physical machine, so change control and review boards should carefully consider each change before approving it, with the same care used on physical production machines. First, any change should be tested in a staging environment to ensure it does not adversely affect either the host or guest operating systems, for example with security tests before and after the change, from a simple port scan to a full vulnerability scan. 2.summary: Patch management in a virtual environment means patching the host and guest operating systems, the software applications and the virtualization software itself, not only the perceived big targets.
2.deeper: A common problem in many organizations, even before virtualization, is patching efforts that focus only on perceived big targets: the operating system and possibly server software such as Web servers, application servers and database servers. The smaller, seemingly inconsequential components, especially those from third parties or open-source libraries, tend to be forgotten, and that can expose the network infrastructure to several critical security issues. At a minimum the host and guest operating systems, the software applications, the hypervisor (VMM) and other virtualized software must be patched. Other components may need patching too, including management software for the virtual machines and software on end-user workstations that lets them run virtual machines.
2.analogy: Patch management is like servicing a vehicle: the engine gets attention, but a worn hose or a loose clamp can stop the vehicle just as surely.
2.scenario: An airman's team patches the host's operating system and the database server. A review finds that an open-source library used by the virtualization software was never patched, so the airman adds it, the hypervisor and the guest operating systems to the patch list.

2.summary: A host operating system is the primary operating system on a computer system's hard drive; in a hosted virtualization solution, the hypervisor runs on top of it.
2.deeper:
The term host OS is usually used when discussing virtualized servers. The National Institute of Standards and Technology defines a host OS as the operating system that the hypervisor runs on top of within a hosted virtualization solution, and the term most commonly describes the operating system that interacts with the hardware and runs a Type 2 hypervisor. The term can also describe an operating system that uses container-based virtualization: the containers share it. A Type 1 hypervisor, in contrast, takes the place of the host OS. One case can confuse: on a server running VMware's ESXi Type 1 hypervisor, a VM's Linux guest OS can create containers that share the Linux kernel, so that guest OS can also be considered a host OS.

Guest OS: virtualization creates multiple virtual operating systems known as guest operating systems. A guest OS is installed on virtual computer architecture and allows end-user interaction indistinguishable from a standard physical computer. A single virtual environment can consist of more than one guest OS, assuming the physical machine has sufficient hardware capacity and memory, and a guest OS need not be the same as the host OS: OS X can be the host while Windows 10 on a VM is the guest.
2.analogy: The host OS is like the landlord's own home in a building with rented flats: it is there first, it owns the foundation, and the tenants' flats are built on top.
2.scenario: An airman's computer runs OS X from its hard drive: that is the host operating system. The airman adds a hosted hypervisor on top of it and creates a VM running Windows 10: the guest operating system.
2.example: The family that owns a house lives in it first, and lodgers stay in rooms the family provides. The host OS is that owner. In the course: A host operating system is the primary operating system on a computer system's hard drive, Block Text p.25.

2.summary: Containers are logical partitions used to separate applications on the same server; they share the kernel of the host OS and need no guest OS and no hypervisor.
2.deeper:
Containerization is a virtualization technique that relies on neither a guest operating system nor a virtual machine. While VMs are all about virtualizing hardware, containers are more like virtualizing an operating system. Applications run inside containers, which are much smaller than VMs, and the applications are tricked into thinking they run on a dedicated instance of the operating system. All the containers share the same base operating system, the host OS: they are spun up from the same base set, which makes bringing new containers online extremely fast, and they share the same kernel resources. Containers are smaller, lighter and faster than VMs. Whereas VMs isolate the guest OS and applications, a container does not, so the applications in a container must be compatible with the underlying host OS because they rely on its kernel.

Operating-System-Level Virtualization: a server virtualization method in which the kernel of the host operating system allows multiple isolated user-space instances called containers. It gives greater efficiency than VMs but less flexibility: the container OS must match the host server's.
2.analogy: Containers are like rooms in one house sharing a single kitchen and plumbing: each room is private, but all of them must work with the same pipes. VMs are more like separate houses.
2.scenario: An airman must run several small applications on one Linux server, each kept apart from the others and quick to bring online. Containers fit: they share the Linux kernel, need no guest OS, and every application must be compatible with that Linux host OS.

2.summary: A Type 2 hypervisor, also known as a hosted hypervisor, runs on top of a host operating system rather than interacting directly with the hardware.
2.deeper: It is software that manages resources and events for virtual environments, and it can create multiple VMs that each run a guest operating system; the guest operating systems need not be the same as the host OS. A hosted hypervisor requires an OS to be installed first. That gives better hardware compatibility than bare-metal virtualization, because the OS is responsible for the hardware drivers instead of the hypervisor. The disadvantage: it has no direct access to hardware and must go through the OS, which increases memory and processor usage and can degrade virtual machine performance; the hypervisor must also balance resources and prioritizes the software and applications on the host OS. Hosted hypervisors are common for desktops, since they allow running multiple operating systems, and they are popular with developers to keep application compatibility on modern operating systems. Examples: Oracle VM VirtualBox, VMware Workstation and VMware Fusion.
2.analogy: A Type 2 hypervisor is like a tenant who sublets rooms: everything goes through the landlord first, which is convenient, but each request takes a little longer.
2.scenario: A user's computer runs OS X, but an application the user needs is available only for Windows. The user installs VMware Fusion, a Type 2 hypervisor, on OS X, creates a VM with Windows 10 as its guest operating system, and runs the Windows application inside that VM.

2.summary: A Type 1 hypervisor, also known as a bare-metal hypervisor, is installed directly onto a server's hardware, where it takes the place of the host OS.
2.deeper: It is software that manages resources and events for virtual environments, and it can create virtual machines, each of which may run a guest operating system. Because it installs on the machine hardware, it is said to reside on bare metal. Residing on the bare metal allows direct access to hardware resources, which results in better performance, scalability and stability, with decreased memory and processor usage compared to Type 2. One disadvantage is that hardware support is typically more limited, because the hypervisor usually has limited built-in device drivers. Bare-metal virtualization is well suited for data centers because it usually comes with advanced features for resource management, high availability and security, and administrators can manage it centrally, which is critical when there are many hosts in the virtual infrastructure. Examples: VMware ESXi and Microsoft Hyper-V.
2.analogy: A Type 1 hypervisor is like a building manager who owns the building outright: no landlord stands between the manager and the boiler room, so things get done directly.
2.scenario: A data center with many hosts needs central management, high availability and security. The administrators install a bare-metal hypervisor directly on each server's hardware, with no host OS, and manage all the hosts from one place.

3.summary: Windows Server is the version of Microsoft's operating system the Air Force currently uses; it provides a highly secure network infrastructure, and Active Directory is proprietary to it.
3.deeper:
Windows Server is the version of Microsoft's operating system currently used by the Air Force. Designed to power the next generation of networks, applications and Web services, it helps administrators develop, deliver and manage rich user experiences and applications. It provides a highly secure network infrastructure and increases technological efficiency within an organization. Its features make it a versatile operating system: centralized administration, centralized management of resources, security, scalability and compatibility, reliability, and fault tolerance and recovery.

Part of Windows Server is the use of domains: in a Windows domain, user accounts, computers and printers are registered in a central database on one or more domain controllers. Active Directory, the directory service that stores information on all network resources, is proprietary to Windows Server.

3.summary: Active Directory is a directory service, proprietary to Windows Server, that stores information about all network resources across a domain and lets users quickly find them.
3.deeper:
Active Directory (AD) is a directory service, not just a directory. It stores information about all network resources, such as servers, printers, individual user accounts, groups of user accounts and security policies, across a domain. It is an advanced hierarchical directory service proprietary to Microsoft, used for managing permissions and user and group access to network resources. As a directory service, it provides a central listing of resources and ways to quickly find and access them, so users do not have to keep track of which server holds which resource. From an administrator's point of view, it is a simple, hierarchical design administered from a single location.

Its structure is tree-like, like the hierarchy of folders and subfolders: it consists of forests, trees, domains, organizational units, objects and sites. Just as files are the basic elements grouped in folders and subfolders, objects are the basic elements of Active Directory.

Directory: a directory is a list organizing resources and their associated characteristics, like a telephone directory. A file system directory organizes files and their characteristics, such as file size, owner, type and permissions. Active Directory uses the same idea for the resources of a network.
3.analogy: A plain directory is like a printed phone book: a list you read yourself. Active Directory is more like an information desk that holds the list and also points you to what you need, so you never have to know which room it is kept in.
3.scenario: An airman needs to print a report but does not know which server holds the squadron's printer. Active Directory keeps a central listing of the network's resources, so the airman finds the printer by searching for it instead of tracking which server holds it.
3.example: A library catalog lists every book with its details, so a reader finds one without walking every shelf. 3.summary: The logical structure of Active Directory groups objects based on how they logically function together, so a resource is found by its name rather than its physical location.
3.deeper: The Active Directory service provides both logical and physical structures for grouping network components. The logical structure is the groupings of objects based on how they logically function together. Grouping resources logically enables finding a resource by its name rather than its physical location. Its parts are the partitions (configuration, schema and domain), the tree, the forest, the organizational unit, the forest root, the object, the child domain and the leaf. The physical structure is the other side: the LANs, WANs and MANs that connect the domains, with sites, domain controllers, global catalog servers, member servers and domain clients.
3.analogy: The logical structure is like the contact list on a phone, sorted by name and group; the physical structure is like the towers and wires that carry the call. You find a person by name without knowing which tower carries the call.
3.scenario: MSgt Rush groups the base's users, computers and printers by the work they do together. An airman looking for a printer then finds it by its name in that grouping, not by the building it sits in.
3.example: A store shelves its products under aisle signs such as Bakery and Produce, so shoppers find what they need by its kind, not by the warehouse it came from. In the course: the logical structure is groupings of objects based on how they logically function together, Block Text p.33.

3.summary: A directory partition is where Active Directory information is segregated and logically stored; the three are configuration, schema and domain.
3.deeper:
A directory partition is where Active Directory information is segregated and logically stored, and partitions are part of the logical structure of Active Directory. Each partition holds one kind of information. The schema partition contains the schema container, which stores class and attribute definitions for all existing and possible Active Directory objects. The domain partition contains a container for one domain, which stores the users, computers, groups and other objects of that specific domain.

Configuration partition: it contains the configuration container, which stores configuration objects for the entire forest: the replication topology and other configuration data that must be replicated throughout the forest. Every domain controller in the forest has a replica of the same configuration partition, and the domain controllers can be set to update periodically so they share the same configuration settings.
3.analogy: Directory partitions are like the three drawers of one filing cabinet: one for the settings every office shares, one for the blank forms that say what each record must hold, and one for this office's own records.
3.scenario: An airman looks for where the user accounts of the base's domain are kept. They are not in the configuration partition, which holds forest-wide configuration, or in the schema partition, which holds class and attribute definitions. They are in the domain partition of that domain.
3.example: A school keeps its timetable, its blank enrollment form and its student files in separate places, so each kind of information is easy to find. In the course: a directory partition is where the AD information is segregated and logically stored, Block Text p.33.

3.summary: The schema is a set of object classes, attributes and syntaxes that defines each type of object in Active Directory and the rules for creating and modifying objects with consistency.
3.deeper: The schema for Active Directory consists of a set of object classes, attributes and syntaxes stored in containers. It also defines rules that ensure objects are created and modified with consistency. Each type of object in Active Directory is defined through the schema, which is the template of attributes, like a small database of information associated with that object. For example, a user account schema could be made up of logon name, password, organization and email address. The schema partition stores class and attribute definitions for all existing and possible Active Directory objects; the objects themselves, such as the users, computers and groups of a domain, are stored in the domain partition of that domain. The trees of a forest share a common directory schema.
3.analogy: The schema is like a blank form: it says which boxes every record of that kind must have. Filling in the form for each person makes the records, and because everyone uses the same form, every record has the same boxes.
3.scenario: An airman creates two new user accounts. Both get the same fields, such as logon name, password, organization and email address, because the schema is the template that defines the user object and keeps objects created with consistency.
3.example: A blank job application has the same boxes for every applicant, so each finished form lists the same kinds of information. In the course: The schema for Active Directory consists of a set of object classes, attributes, and syntaxes, Block Text p.34.

3.summary: A domain is a group of users, servers and other resources sharing a centralized database of account and security information.
3.deeper:
A domain is a logical structure based on the requirements of an organization: a group of users, servers and other resources sharing a centralized database of account and security information. Domains are established on a network to make it easier to organize and manage resources and security. In a Windows domain, user accounts, computers and printers are registered in a central database located on one or more domain controllers, which gives administrators a way to manage large numbers of PCs and control them from one location.

A domain is not confined by geographical or physical boundaries: it can represent users and computers at a single physical location or in many locations. Each domain can have its own security policies and can establish trust relationships with other domains. Active Directory may be made up of one or more domains.
3.analogy: A domain is like a club with one membership roll: its members may live in different towns, but one roll and one set of club rules covers them all. A second club keeps its own roll and rules, and the two clubs can agree to trust each other's members.
3.scenario: MSgt Rush shows an airman a domain whose users work at two locations. The users at both places log on against the same central database of account and security information, because a domain is not confined by physical boundaries.
3.example: A company's staff list and badge rules apply to every employee, whether they work at headquarters or at a branch office. In the course: a Domain is also a group of users, servers, and other resources sharing a centralized database of account and security information, Block Text p.35.

3.summary: A domain tree is a collection of one or more domains that share a common namespace, with a root domain at its base and child domains branching out from it.
3.deeper: A domain tree is a collection of one or more domains that share a common namespace. The fx.movie.edu and movie.edu domains, for example, are both part of the movie.edu domain tree. Active Directory organizes multiple domains hierarchically in a tree structure. At the base is the root domain, or parent. From the root domain, child domains branch out to separate groups of objects with the same security policies. Under the child domains, multiple organizational units branch out to further subdivide the network systems. A forest is the collection of one or more domain trees.
3.analogy: A domain tree is like a family that shares one surname: the parent is at the base, the children branch out from it, and every member shares the family name, the way the domains of a tree share a common namespace.
3.scenario: An airman reads two domain names, movie.edu and fx.movie.edu. Both belong to one domain tree, the movie.edu domain tree, because a domain tree is a collection of domains that share a common namespace. At the base of any such tree is the root domain, or parent, and child domains branch out from it.
3.example: Houses in one town all share the town's name in their address. In the course: A domain tree is simply a collection of one or more domains that share a common namespace, Block Text p.35.

3.summary: A forest is the collection of one or more domain trees at the top of the Active Directory structure; its trees share a global catalog, directory schema, logical structure and directory configuration.
3.deeper: At the top of the Active Directory structure is the forest: the collection of one or more domain trees. A forest is a collection of trees sharing a common global catalog, directory schema, logical structure and directory configuration. The forest represents the security boundary within which users, computers, groups and other objects are accessible; it is the outermost boundary of the directory service. The first domain created in the forest is the forest root domain. Inside the forest, each domain can still have its own security policies and its own organizational unit hierarchy.
3.analogy: A forest is like a whole base: several units run their own sections, but all of them use one base directory and one set of base-wide definitions, and the base fence is the outer boundary.
3.scenario: An airman studies a design with two domain trees, each with its own namespace. Both trees share one global catalog, one directory schema, one logical structure and one directory configuration, so they belong to the same forest, the outermost boundary of that directory service.
3.example: Two neighborhoods inside one fenced community have different street names but share one gate and one community map. In the course: A forest is a collection of trees sharing a common global catalog, directory schema, logical structure, and directory configuration, Block Text p.36.

3.summary: The forest root domain is the first domain created in an Active Directory forest; it provides the foundation for the Active Directory infrastructure.
3.deeper:
The first domain created in an Active Directory forest is automatically designated as the forest root domain. It provides the foundation for the Active Directory infrastructure, and it must be created before any of the regional domains. Services running on the forest root domain controllers must be highly available to ensure users maintain access to resources throughout the forest. The forest owner is responsible for deploying it.

If the forest design requires only one domain, the forest root domain also contains all users, groups and resources. In a multiple-domain design, the forest root domain can be a dedicated root used only for administration of the forest, or it can contain users, groups and resources in addition to the forest administration accounts. Administrators can create an organizational unit structure after the forest root domain deployment is complete, and the forest owner then creates one or more regional domains to complete the forest hierarchy.
3.analogy: The forest root domain is like the foundation poured before a building's walls go up: it comes first, and everything else is built on it.
3.scenario: An airman helps the forest owner deploy a new forest. The first domain created becomes the forest root domain. Only after it is deployed does the forest owner create the regional domains that complete the forest hierarchy.
3.example: The cornerstone of a building is laid before any other stone of the wall. In the course: The first domain created in the AD forest is automatically designated as the forest root domain, Block Text p.36.

3.summary: An object is the basic element of Active Directory: it represents one thing on the network, such as a user, a group, a computer, an application, a printer or a shared folder.
3.deeper:
An object is the basic element of Active Directory and represents something on the network, such as a user, a group, a computer, an application, a printer or a shared folder. An object represents a single entity and its attributes, and everything stored in Active Directory is stored as an object. Every object in an Active Directory domain is given a Globally Unique Identifier when it is created; the number stays with the object and helps Active Directory catalog everything. Objects can be organized into object classes or logical object groupings. Some objects are container objects that can hold other objects: organizational units and domains are examples.

Attributes: attributes define the types of information an object can hold; they define and describe the object. The attributes of a user object might include the user's name, e-mail address and phone number. All objects of the same type or class have the same set of attributes, but they are told apart by different values for at least one of them.

Leaf: a leaf describes an endpoint of a branch in Active Directory. Leaf objects, or terminal objects, are found in containers such as organizational units and cannot contain other directory objects; a leaf signifies an endpoint of a tree or subtree.
3.analogy: In a filing system, folders hold other folders and files, but a file holds no folders. Container objects are like folders, a leaf is like a file at the end of the path, and the details written on the file's label are like its attributes.
3.scenario: An airman opens an organizational unit called Users and finds a user object for each member of the base network. Each user object carries the same set of attributes, such as name, e-mail address and phone number, but with different values. The user objects hold no other objects, so each one is a leaf.
3.example: Each card in a recipe box is one item, and the lines on the card describe that item. In the course: An object is the basic element of Active Directory in Microsoft Windows that represents something on the network, Block Text p.37.

3.summary: The physical structure of Active Directory defines how domains are physically connected: the LANs, WANs and MANs that make up and connect them.
3.deeper: When Active Directory is designed, its physical structure needs consideration. The physical structure defines how the domains are physically connected or structured to each other: the LANs, WANs and MANs (local, wide and metropolitan area networks) that make up and connect domains. How the domains physically connect affects the efficiency of replication among the domain controllers. Its parts are sites, domain controllers, global catalog servers, member servers and domain clients. A site maps the physical structure of a network, while domains map the logical structure of an organization; domains can span geography with different topologies connected by WAN links and still be transparent to the user.
3.analogy: The logical structure is like an organization chart; the physical structure is like the roads between the buildings. The chart decides who belongs together; the roads affect how well things move between them.
3.scenario: An airman sees a domain that spans two bases connected by a WAN link. Users at both bases see one domain, but the domain controllers at the two bases replicate over that link, and how the domains physically connect affects how efficiently they replicate.

3.summary: A site maps the physical structure of a network and is defined as a range of IP subnets; domains, by contrast, map the logical structure of an organization.
3.deeper:
A site maps the physical structure of a network, where domains map the logical structure of an organization. Active Directory sites are defined as a range of IP subnets, and a network can be a geographically separated WAN between cities or bases. Two sites can be part of the same domain but on different networks: domains can span geography with different topologies connected by WAN links and still be transparent to the user. Windows encourages the use of sites when a network is divided by a slow link.

If multiple networks in close proximity have fast, reliable connections, all their subnets can go in a single site: when the round-trip network latency between two servers in different subnets is 10 ms or less, both subnets can be in the same site, and when it is greater than 10 ms, they should not be in a single site. Even when latency is 10 ms or less, separate sites may be deployed to segment the traffic between sites for Active Directory-based applications. Active Directory permits multiple sites within a single domain or a single site serving multiple domains.
3.analogy: Domains are like teams on an organization chart; sites are like buildings on a map. One team can work in two buildings, and one building can hold several teams.
3.scenario: An airman maps two subnets at the same base with fast, reliable connections; the round-trip latency between their servers is 10 ms or less, so they share one site. A subnet at a distant base, reached over a slow link with latency greater than 10 ms, gets a site of its own.
3.example: A delivery map groups nearby streets into one route and gives a distant town its own route, whatever company each house belongs to. In the course: A site maps the physical structure of a network where domains map the logical structure of an organization, Block Text p.39.

3.summary: A domain controller is a Windows Server that manages the domain security policy and authenticates users and computers before they access resources in the domain.
3.deeper:
A domain controller is a Microsoft Windows Server that manages the domain security policy. Users and computers that need access to network resources within the domain must be authenticated by a domain controller in the domain. Domain controllers are also responsible for authenticating users, enforcing policies and replication. It manages information in the Active Directory database and enables users to log on to the domain, be authenticated for accessing resources in the domain, and search the directory for information about users and network resources. Domain controllers are the most important servers on a network; without them there is no structure. A network normally has more than one, so if one fails, others store the Active Directory structure and authenticate users.

Member server: a member server belongs to a domain but is not the domain controller. Member servers are usually used for dedicated network purposes, such as file and print servers, application servers, database servers or web servers.
3.analogy: A domain controller is like the front desk of a secured building: it checks each badge against the building's records before anyone goes in, and more than one desk stays open so one closed desk does not lock everyone out. A member server is like an office inside the building with one job, such as the mail room.
3.scenario: An airman logs on at a domain client at the start of a shift. A domain controller authenticates the airman against the Active Directory database before any file share in the domain opens. The share itself sits on a member server: it belongs to the domain but is not the domain controller.
3.example: A gate guard checks each ID against the access roster before anyone drives onto the base. In the course: A domain controller is a Microsoft Windows Server that manages the domain security policy, Block Text p.40.

3.summary: A global catalog server includes Active Directory objects from all domains in a forest, so computers in one domain can locate and access resources in another.
3.deeper: Each domain controller includes objects and object attributes unique to its own domain. To allow access to network resources in other domains within a tree or forest, those resources must first be located, and a global catalog server does that. Global catalog servers include Active Directory objects from all domains in a forest: a global catalog server stores a full replica of every object within its own domain and a partial replica of each object within every domain in the forest. This allows computers in one domain to locate and access resources in a different domain. A global catalog server must be available so users can log on and locate Active Directory resources, and at least one per site is recommended to speed up these processes. It is part of the physical structure of Active Directory.
3.analogy: A domain controller is like a squadron's own roster. A global catalog server is like the base directory: full details for its own squadron and a short entry for every member of every other squadron, enough to find anyone on base.

4.summary: The Domain Name System (DNS) resolves host names to IP addresses and back; it is made of three components that work together: resolvers, resource records and name servers.
4.deeper:
DNS resolves host names to IP addresses, and IP addresses back to names. Host names are much easier for people to remember than IP addresses when connecting to another system. If a computer cannot access DNS, its web browser will not be able to find websites, and email cannot be sent or received. The DNS service does not rely on one file or even one server, but on many computers across the globe.

To direct traffic efficiently, DNS consists of three components. A resolver is software on a TCP/IP host that queries a name server. Resource records are the entries in a DNS database that hold information about domain names. Name servers contain databases of associated names and IP addresses and provide that information to resolvers on request. Active Directory depends on DNS too: it uses DNS to locate networked computers, such as Domain Controllers, by resolving computer names to IP addresses.
4.analogy: DNS is like a phone directory service. People remember names, not numbers; the caller's assistant asks the directory office, which looks the name up in its listings and reads back the number.
4.scenario: An airman types a website's name into a browser. The resolver built into the browser queries a name server, the name server answers from the resource records in its database, and the browser gets the IP address it needs to reach the site.
4.example: A contacts list lets a person tap a friend's name instead of remembering the number behind it. In the course: DNS resolves host names to IP addresses, Block Text p.47.

4.summary: A resolver is software running on a TCP/IP host that lets the host query a name server and resolve a host name into its IP address.
4.deeper:
Abstractly, a resolver is any host or client on the Internet that needs to look up domain name information. More concretely, it is software running on a TCP/IP host that enables the host to query a name server to resolve a host name into its associated IP address. The resolver client is built into TCP/IP applications such as web browsers, email clients and any other programs that need name-to-IP address resolution to communicate on the network and the Internet.

The resolver works in four steps: a program, such as a browser, requests DNS information from the resolver; the resolver sends a query to the local name server; it interprets the response from the local name server; and it passes this information to the program that initially called the resolver software.
4.analogy: A resolver is like an assistant who takes a question from the boss, phones the right office, makes sense of the reply, and brings the answer back to the boss's desk.
4.scenario: An airman opens a web browser and types a site's name. The browser asks its built-in resolver, which queries the local name server, reads the response, and hands the IP address back to the browser so it can connect.
4.example: A travel app asks its map service for a place's location, then shows the answer to the person who asked. In the course: a resolver is software running on a TCP/IP host that enables the host to query a name server to resolve a host name into its associated IP address, Block Text p.47.

4.summary: A resource record is an individual entry in a DNS database that contains information about domain names; the resolver uses these records to match a host name to its IP address.
4.deeper:
A resource record is an individual entry in a DNS database that contains information about domain names in DNS; it identifies the hosts, also known as nodes, residing within the network. Records in the DNS database file match up host names and IP addresses for nodes on a network, and the resolver uses these records to match up the host name to the IP address.

Common record types: A (address) maps the host name to the IP address. CNAME (canonical name) creates an alias for a host name. SOA (start of authority) indicates admin information for an authoritative name server. Service (SRV) locates a host that can provide a specific network service. HINFO (host information) specifies information about the host, such as its operating system and CPU type.

NS Record: an NS (name server) record indicates a DNS name server that is authoritative for the domain.
4.analogy: A DNS database is like a card file. Each card is one record, and the card's type says what is on it: an address, a nickname, who runs the office, or where to find a service.
4.scenario: An airman's browser needs the IP address of a server on base. The resolver's query reaches the name server, which looks in its DNS database file and finds the A record that maps that host name to its IP address.

4.summary: Name servers provide the namespace of all hosts on the Internet or a private TCP/IP network: they contain databases of names and IP addresses and give this information to resolvers on request.
4.deeper:
Name servers are an essential component of DNS. Because of them, you can reach a host on a TCP/IP network by its friendly DNS name instead of its IP address. They contain databases of associated names and IP addresses and provide this information to the resolvers on request, and they are distributed all over the Internet and within organizations to answer DNS queries. The name server roles are primary, secondary and caching-only.

Primary Name Server: contains the master copy of the zone file for the zones it has authority over. When it shares zone files with another name server, it is performing the master name server role.

Secondary Name Server: obtains its zone files using a zone transfer from the primary (master) name server. Its zone copies are read only.

Authoritative Name Server: a name server that can answer queries based on the resource records stored in the zones it maintains. Primary and secondary name servers are both authoritative for their zones. A caching-only name server is not: it contains no zone information and keeps cached queries until their TTL expires.
4.analogy: Name servers are like the offices of a records department. The head office keeps the master file; branch offices keep read-only copies sent from the head office; both can answer questions about their own files. A help desk with no files of its own just remembers recent answers for a while.
4.scenario: An airman's organization runs a primary name server holding the master copy of its zone file. A second name server gets read-only copies through zone transfers. When a resolver asks about a host in the zone, either one can answer with authority from the records in its zone.
4.example: A school's main office keeps the official student list and sends copies to each department office, and any of them can tell a visitor where a student is. 4.summary: The DNS namespace is the hierarchical, inverted tree structure of DNS: it begins with the root domain and is divided into domains, which divide further until they reach the host name.
4.deeper:
DNS has a hierarchical inverted tree structure, and that structure is called the DNS namespace. It begins with the root domain, which branches to top-level domains, then second-level domains, third-level domains, and so on to the individual host name. The tree is also subdivided into zones, each the part a DNS server is responsible for.

DNS Domain: the namespace is divided into domains, and domains further divide into sub-domains until they reach the host name. For fault tolerance and to reduce network traffic, copies of DNS domain information are often kept on more than one server.

Top-Level Domain: the name servers forming the layer under the root domain. There are many more of them than root servers, and they provide name resolution for endings such as .com, .net, .edu, .mil and .gov.

Second-Level Domain: the name servers forming the layer under the top-level domain, for names such as cisco.com and airforce.mil. Most domain names typically stop at the second level.

Third-Level Domain: often called a subdomain. In large organizations, third-level domains provide division for departments or functions, and they can be used to balance the load on sites with heavy traffic.
4.analogy: The namespace is like a family tree drawn upside down: one ancestor at the top, branches under it, and smaller branches under those, until each line ends at one person. Every name in the tree can be traced back up to the top.
4.scenario: An airman traces airforce.mil in the namespace. Below the root sits the top-level domain .mil; under it, airforce.mil is a second-level domain, where most domain names stop. If the organization were large, a third-level domain, a subdomain, could divide it by department or function on the way down to a host name.

4.summary: A zone is a part of the DNS namespace for which a DNS server is responsible; zones are created to store the DNS records and sub-domains of a domain.
4.deeper:
The DNS namespace is a hierarchical inverted tree, and the tree is subdivided into zones. A zone is a part of the DNS namespace for which a DNS server is responsible. Zones are created to store the DNS records and sub-domains from each domain on the DNS server, and every zone is a part of the DNS namespace, a consistent naming scheme. For example, www.google.com and mail.google.com are part of google.com.

When a zone is created, the administrators designate whether it will hold records for forward lookups or reverse lookups. A name server is authoritative when it can answer queries from the resource records stored in the zones it maintains.
4.analogy: A zone is like one county on a map of a country: the whole map is the namespace, and each county office is responsible for the streets and houses inside its own border.
