4.summary: A zone transfer is the process of moving information from the primary zone to the secondary zone, so DNS servers stay synchronized automatically.
4.deeper:
For fault tolerance and to reduce network traffic, it is often useful to keep copies of DNS domain information on more than one server. When DNS information is stored on multiple servers, it is essential that the servers automatically synchronize information among themselves. If the information gets out of synchronization, replication of Active Directory may be affected, and clients may be prevented from logging on to the network. From an administrative point of view it is also convenient to automate this, to save time and effort.

Primary and secondary zones are traditionally used for this. The primary zone database is the master copy of the zone database file, located on the primary DNS server for the zone and stored as a standard text file. The secondary zone database is a copy of the primary zone database, stored as a read-only text file. The process of moving information from the primary zone to the secondary zone is called a zone transfer.
4.analogy: A zone transfer is like a head office sending updated copies of its master price list to each branch, so every branch quotes the same prices and none of them edits the list itself.
4.scenario: An airman's organization keeps its DNS domain information on two servers for fault tolerance. The primary DNS server holds the master copy of the zone; the secondary server receives a read-only copy through zone transfers, so both answer the same way. If the two ever fell out of sync, Active Directory replication could suffer and clients could be unable to log on.
4.example: A shared calendar updates every team member's copy from one master calendar, so nobody works from an old date. In the course: the process of moving information from the primary zone to the secondary zone is called a zone transfer, Block Text p.51.

4.summary: The root domain is the name servers forming the upper-most layer of the DNS namespace; it is reached through 13 server addresses backed by clusters of servers around the world.
4.deeper:
The DNS namespace begins with the root domain, the name servers that form its upper-most layer; it branches to the top-level domains below it. The root is reached through 13 server addresses, located world-wide.

A common misconception is that there are only 13 physical root servers in the world. In reality there are many more, but still only 13 IP addresses used to query the different root server networks: limitations in the original architecture of DNS require a maximum of 13 server addresses in the root zone. In the early days of the Internet there was only one server for each of the 13 IP addresses, most of them in the United States. Today each of the 13 addresses has clusters of servers, which distribute requests based on load and proximity, and there are over 600 DNS root servers across every populated continent.

The layer under the root is the top-level domain, made up of many more name servers, providing name resolution for .com, .edu, .gov, .net and so on.
4.analogy: The root is like a national help line with a short, fixed list of phone numbers: callers only ever dial those few numbers, but behind each one sits a whole call center spread across many cities, taking the call nearest or least busy.
4.scenario: An airman reads that the DNS root has only 13 addresses and assumes there are only 13 root machines. MSgt Rush corrects the idea: the 13 addresses remain because of the original DNS architecture, but each one fronts clusters of servers, over 600 in all, that share requests by load and proximity.
4.example: One customer-service number can ring at many offices in different cities, the call going to the nearest or least busy one. In the course: name servers forming the upper-most layer of the DNS namespace hierarchy, Unit 4 Slides p.23.

4.summary: A fully qualified domain name (FQDN) is the complete domain name for a specific computer, or host, specifying its exact location in the DNS tree.
4.deeper:
The FQDN is the complete domain name for a specific computer, or host, on the internet. It is also called an absolute domain name, because it specifies its exact location in the tree hierarchy of DNS: it covers all the domain levels that apply.

To map an FQDN to the DNS hierarchy, start at the right side with the top-level domain, then proceed left to the second level, the third level, and so on until you reach the end of the subdomains for the object in question. The root is not written: it is automatically assumed, because every fully qualified domain name has a root. The goal of DNS is to resolve an FQDN to an IP address.
4.analogy: An FQDN is like a full mailing address read from the largest part to the smallest: country, then city, then street, then the house. A street name alone could be anywhere; the full address points to one house.

4.summary: Name resolution is the process DNS uses to resolve a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) to an IP address, the goal of DNS.
4.deeper:
The goal of DNS is to resolve a fully qualified domain name to an IP address, using a process called name resolution: for example, what is the IP address for www.example.com? Active Directory relies on it too, locating networked computers by resolving computer names to IP addresses.

If the host or its resolver doesn't know the answer, it asks the local name server. If the local name server doesn't know it either, it tries to locate the authoritative name server for that zone using a DNS query. Several requests can be required to resolve a single name, so to keep traffic to a minimum the local name server caches the results of its queries. The cache also lets it answer other queries for the same domain space more quickly. Cached entries are kept only for a limited amount of time.
4.analogy: Finding a number by asking around: you ask the person at the next desk; if they don't know, they call around until they reach someone who does, and they jot the number on a sticky note in case someone else asks soon.
4.scenario: An airman's computer needs the IP address for www.example.com. Its resolver doesn't know it, so it asks the local name server. That server doesn't know either, so it uses a DNS query to locate the authoritative name server for the zone, then caches the answer for a while so the next query for that domain is faster.

4.summary: A DNS query, also known as a lookup, is the technical term for the search used in name resolution, from a name to an IP address or from an IP address to a name.
4.deeper:
The goal of DNS is to resolve a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) to an IP address. A DNS query is the technical term for the search used in that name resolution process: a name-to-IP address request is a forward lookup, and an IP address-to-name request is a reverse lookup. There are three types of DNS query: recursive, iterative and non-recursive.

Recursive Query: a client provides a hostname, and the DNS resolver must provide an answer. It responds with either a relevant resource record or an error message if the record can't be found.

In an iterative query the resolver returns the best answer it can, while the local DNS server starts from the root and works down the hierarchy. In a non-recursive query the resolver already knows the answer, because the record is stored in the device's OS or the authoritative server is known, so the response is returned at once with no more rounds of queries.
4.analogy: Asking for a phone number can go three ways. One helper must come back with the number or say it doesn't exist; another gives the best lead it has; and sometimes the helper already knows the number by heart and answers at once.
4.scenario: An airman's browser needs the IP address of a host. The resolver sends a DNS query to the local DNS server. As a recursive query, the resolver must come back with the record or an error message; as an iterative query, the local DNS server works down from the root and the resolver returns the best answer it can.

4.summary: A forward lookup zone holds the records that resolve a hostname to an IP address, the most common task a DNS server performs.
4.deeper:
The most common task a DNS server performs is resolving a hostname to an IP address; this is called a forward lookup. When a zone is created, the administrators designate whether it will hold records for forward lookups or reverse lookups.

Resolving hostnames within an organization is a two-packet process. The first packet is a request from the DNS client to the DNS server containing the hostname to be resolved. The second packet is the response from the server to the client containing the IP address of the requested hostname. The forward lookup database is made up of resource records such as A, CNAME and MX that enable the name-to-IP address resolution. A reverse lookup zone does the opposite: it resolves IP addresses to hostnames.
4.analogy: A forward lookup is like looking up a name in a phone book to get the number. The reverse, finding whose name goes with a number, is a different book.
4.scenario: An airman's computer needs the IP address of a printer on base. The DNS client sends one packet to the DNS server with the printer's hostname, and the server's response packet carries the IP address, taken from the records in the forward lookup zone.
4.example: Finding a classmate's room number by looking up the name on a dorm list goes from the name to the number. In the course: the most common task a DNS server performs is resolving a hostname to an IP address, called a forward lookup, Block Text p.50.

4.summary: In an iterative query, a DNS client provides a hostname and the DNS resolver returns the best answer it can, while the local DNS server works down the hierarchy from the root.
4.deeper:
In an iterative query, a DNS client provides a hostname, and the DNS resolver returns the best answer it can. The resolver begins by querying the organization's local DNS server, which assumes responsibility for the resolution. If it does not have the record, the local DNS server starts an iterative query process, starting from the DNS root server, then going to a top-level domain server, and continuing down the hierarchy until it finds the authoritative name server that holds the IP address and other information for the requested hostname. The local DNS server retains responsibility throughout the search.

Compare a recursive query, in which the resolver must provide an answer: a relevant resource record or an error message.
4.analogy: It is like a desk clerk who takes your question and keeps it: the clerk calls the head office, then the regional office, then the local branch, until someone has the answer, and you only ever talk to the clerk.

The local server asks a root server, then a top-level domain server, and keeps going down until it reaches the authoritative name server holding the IP address; the resolver then returns the best answer it can.

5.summary: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) is a client-server protocol: DHCP servers lease IP addresses and other TCP/IP information to the DHCP clients that request them.
5.deeper:
DHCP is designed to reduce configuration time for TCP/IP networks: the program manages IP address allocation for the network. It is a client-server protocol that uses DHCP servers and DHCP clients. DHCP consists of a scope, or pool, of IP addresses, and the process by which a client obtains an address is called DORA. Information about scopes and leased IP addresses is stored in the DHCP database on the DHCP server. Errors in configuring the DHCP scope are a common reason for problems in establishing communication on TCP/IP networks.

DHCP Server: a machine that runs a service that can lease out IP addresses and other TCP/IP information to any client that requests them. It typically has a pool of IP addresses, known as a scope, that it is allowed to distribute to clients.

DHCP Options: assign DHCP options to the DHCP server if clients need them; at the Ack step, the server assigns the client any configured DHCP options.
5.analogy: DHCP is like a hotel front desk: guests ask for a room, the desk hands out a key from the rooms it holds, writes the stay in its register, and adds a card with the useful numbers for the stay.
5.scenario: A new workstation joins an airman's network and asks for its settings. The DHCP server leases it an IP address from its scope, records the lease in its DHCP database, and assigns it any configured DHCP options.
5.example: A school office hands each new student a locker number, records it in its book, and gives a sheet with the bell times, so no student has to work these out alone. In the course: DHCP is a client-server protocol that uses DHCP servers and DHCP clients, Block Text p.61.

5.summary: A scope is a range of IP addresses that a DHCP server can lease out to DHCP clients; on a network with several DHCP servers, each scope must be unique.
5.deeper:
The DHCP server typically has a pool of IP addresses, known as a scope, that it is allowed to distribute to clients. The values for IP address scopes must be taken from the available pool of IP addresses allocated to the network. When administrators create scopes on multiple DHCP servers, each scope must be unique, so that the servers do not cause conflicts by leasing duplicate IP addresses: be sure their scopes do not overlap. Static IP addresses for printers or servers can be set aside within a scope by excluding them from the pool. Information about scopes is stored in the DHCP database on the DHCP server.

If one DHCP server must serve hosts on several subnets, configure DHCP relay agents. Errors in configuring the DHCP scope are a common reason for problems in establishing communication on TCP/IP networks.
5.analogy: A scope is like a block of ticket numbers given to one ticket booth. If two booths were given the same block, two people could end up with the same seat, so each booth gets its own block from the venue's numbers.
5.scenario: MSgt Rush plans DHCP for a network with two DHCP servers. Each server gets its own scope, taken from the pool of addresses allocated to the network, and the two scopes do not overlap. Hosts on another subnet are served through a DHCP relay agent.
5.example: A teacher hands each of two helpers a different stack of numbered raffle tickets, so no number is given out twice. In the course: A scope is a range of IP addresses that a DHCP server can lease out to DHCP clients, Block Text p.61.

5.summary: Exclusions are addresses or a range of addresses in a scope that the DHCP server does not distribute, so devices with static IP addresses never get them leased out.
5.deeper:
A scope is the range of IP addresses that a DHCP server can lease out. Administrators can create a pool of static IP addresses within a scope by excluding them from the DHCP pool. Any devices with static IP addresses should be added to the exclusion zone, from the starting to the ending IP address of the static range. This stops DHCP from leasing out static IP addresses, which prevents duplicate IP assignments. The DHCP clients that are dynamic fall within the scope and lease their addresses.

Static IP Address: an address set aside for a device instead of leased. Assign static IP addresses to non-DHCP clients and exclude these addresses from the scope if necessary; set aside static IP addresses for printers and servers. All servers on the network get static IP addresses, or DHCP client reservations so that they always lease the same IP address.
5.analogy: Exclusions are like reserved seats in a theater: the box office sells every seat except the ones marked for the staff, so no ticket ever sends a guest to a seat that is already taken.
5.scenario: An airman builds a scope for a network with a printer, two servers and a non-DHCP client, all with static IP addresses. She adds that static range to the exclusions, so the DHCP server never leases one of those addresses to a workstation and no two devices end up with the same IP address.
5.example: A parking lot keeps a few marked spots for the same vehicles every day, and the attendant never hands those spots to visitors. In the course: Exclusions are addresses or a range of addresses that are not distributed by the server, Block Text p.63.

5.summary: A DHCP lease is the duration for which a DHCP server loans an IP address to a DHCP client; before the lease expires, the client contacts the server to renew it.
5.deeper:
A client computer configured to use DHCP leases an IP address during the boot process, when networking is initialized. The address comes from the server's pool of IP addresses, its scope, and the client keeps it for a specific period, usually several days. The lease duration can be configured on the server. Once the lease is ready to expire, the client contacts the server to arrange for renewal. A PC enabled for DHCP shows when its lease was obtained and when it expires.

The pool is not endless. If the pool of available IP addresses is used up, machines that are added or moved might be unable to obtain an IP address from a DHCP server, and so they cannot participate in network communication.
5.analogy: A lease works like a library book: the reader borrows it for a set number of days and goes back to renew it before it is due. If every copy is already out, the next reader leaves with nothing.
5.scenario: An airman's workstation boots and, as its networking starts, leases an IP address from the DHCP server for several days. Near the end of that period the workstation contacts the server to renew the lease and keeps working. Later a laptop is added to the network after the pool has been used up; it cannot obtain an address, so it cannot take part in network communication.
5.example: A rental car belongs to the renter only for the days on the agreement, and the renter calls to extend before those days run out. A DHCP lease treats an address the same way. 5.summary: DORA is the four-step process, Discover, Offer, Request and Ack, by which a DHCP client obtains a lease for an IP address from a DHCP server.
5.deeper:
DHCP clients obtain a DHCP lease for an IP address, a subnet mask and various DHCP options from DHCP servers in four steps. DHCP Discover: the client broadcasts a request for a DHCP server. DHCP Offer: DHCP servers on the network offer an address to the client. DHCP Request: the client broadcasts a request to lease an address from one of the offering DHCP servers. DHCP Ack: the DHCP server that the client responds to acknowledges the client, assigns it any configured DHCP options and updates its DHCP database. The client then initializes and binds its TCP/IP protocol stack and can begin network communication.

DHCP Offer: the second step. More than one DHCP server can offer an address, so the client chooses one of the offering servers in its request. A server can be set with a delay, the time by which it holds back its DHCPOFFER message; with multiple DHCP servers, the delay gives one server an opportunity to respond before the other sends an offer.
5.analogy: DORA is like asking a room who can lend you a seat: you call out, a few people offer one, you say out loud whose seat you will take, and that person confirms it and writes your name down.
5.scenario: An airman's laptop joins the network and broadcasts a Discover. Two DHCP servers each answer with an Offer. The laptop broadcasts a Request to lease the address from one of them, and that server sends the Ack, assigns the configured DHCP options and updates its DHCP database. The laptop binds its TCP/IP protocol stack and starts communicating.
5.example: Booking a table often runs the same way: a diner calls around, restaurants offer a time, the diner asks one to hold it, and that one confirms and writes the name in its book. 6.summary: Logical security consists of software safeguards for an organization's systems: user identification, password access, authenticating, access rights and authority levels.
6.deeper:
An organization may have thousands of users and devices inside the boundary of its network, all authorized to use it. How can we be sure they are following the rules? The answer is "trust but verify": internal controls are used to control, prevent, identify and report vulnerabilities at the host and network levels to protect networks. Internal controls include proper account settings, file access permissions and rights.

Logical security is made of software safeguards.Anti-virus software, firewalls, passwords and encryption are all examples of logical security mechanisms. For servers, logical security is implemented by using various types of accounts, along with permissions, rights and Group Policy Objects. A STIG, designed to correct a security vulnerability in hardware or software, also falls under the realm of logical security.
6.analogy: Logical security is like the rules and checks inside a base gate: everyone inside is allowed in, yet badges, passwords and duty rosters still make sure each person only does what they are cleared for.
6.scenario: Every user on an airman's network is authorized, yet the unit still checks that they follow the rules. On the server it sets up user accounts with passwords, gives each account the rights and file permissions its job needs, and keeps anti-virus software and encryption in place. All of these are logical security.
6.example: An office checks each employee's sign-in at the computer, even though all of them already passed the front door. In the course: Logical Security consists of software safeguards for an organization's systems, Block Text p.68.

6.summary: An account is a set of credentials for participating in a network; it identifies the user, and each user needs one to reach resources such as shared folders, printers or applications.
6.deeper:
Accounts provide a way of identifying users on a network, and they are the foundation for network security. In a typical network, each user needs an account to access resources such as shared folders, printers or applications. An administrator or another user with high security privileges typically creates accounts.

Accounts are generally used in server-based (dedicated) networks, where a central computer, such as a domain controller, keeps track of each user's account and grants or denies access to the network based on the credentials the user enters at login. Accounts are used less often in peer-to-peer networks or workgroups, because their security requirements are usually much less stringent. The types of accounts include administrator, user (local user, with the built-in local users Administrator and Guest) and domain user accounts.
6.analogy: An account is like a name badge issued at a gate: the guard checks the badge each time, and what the badge allows decides which doors open.
6.scenario: An airman logs in at a workstation on a server-based network. The domain controller checks the credentials entered at login against the airman's account and grants access, so the shared folders and applications open. A teammate who has no account yet cannot reach them.
6.example: A gym membership card identifies its holder at the front desk, and the desk lets members in to the equipment. In the course: An account is a set of credentials for participating in a network, Block Text p.68.

6.summary: An administrator account allows its holder to make changes that will affect other users; an administrator has full rights and permissions to all resources on a network.
6.deeper:
The administrator is usually responsible for installing, managing and controlling servers and networking components. Administrators can also modify the properties of user accounts and the membership of groups, create and install printers, share resources and assign permissions to those resources. As an administrator, you must create the account and assign applicable rights and permissions before a user can log onto the system or network.

Because an administrator account carries this much power, do not give untrained and inexperienced users an admin account: too many rights can crash the network. On a local computer, the built-in Administrator account allows you to manage the local computer, users, groups and resources.
6.analogy: An administrator account is like the master key of a building: the person who holds it can open every room, change the locks and hand out keys to everyone else.
6.scenario: An airman with an administrator account creates an account for a new teammate, adds it to a group, shares a folder and assigns permissions to it. Only then can the teammate log on and open the folder.
6.example: A building manager can change the locks and hand out keys for every office, while the tenants only open their own doors. In the course: An administrator account is an account that allows you to make changes that will affect other users, Block Text p.69.

6.summary: A user account represents one unique user and stores information about that user, such as the username and password (or PIN) needed for logon authentication.
6.deeper:
A user account can be created on a local computer or on a domain controller. A critical part of the information it stores is the username and password, or the PIN in the case of using the Common Access Card, required for user logon authentication. Each user account must be given a unique name and is identified internally by a unique Security Identifier (SID).

The SID is used for tracking rights and permission assignments. When a user is assigned permissions to an object, the user's SID is stored in the object's ACL along with the specific permissions. As an administrator, you create the account and assign the applicable rights and permissions before the user can log on.
6.analogy: A user account is like a service record: it carries the member's name and a unique number, and every clearance granted to the member is filed against that number, not against the name.
6.scenario: An administrator creates a user account for an airman with a unique username and a PIN for the Common Access Card. The system identifies the account internally by its SID. When the airman is given permissions to a shared folder, the folder's ACL stores that SID with the permissions.

6.summary: A local user account lets the user log into one specific machine and access resources on that machine only; it is usually used on a PC for training or in kiosk mode.
6.deeper:
Users who have a local user account can log on only to the computer on which the account was created. A computer or server supports local user accounts only if it is configured as a domain member server, a workgroup member server or a standalone server. Domain controllers do not support local user accounts: they control access to the entire domain and are maintained strictly by domain accounts. If users require access to the network, they get domain user accounts instead.

Built-in local user accounts are created when Windows Server is first installed as a member server or standalone server. The Administrator account allows you to manage the local computer, users, groups and resources. The Guest account provides a way for users to log on or gain access to resources without a unique local username; most local policies instruct you to disable it. Other built-in local users may be created depending on what services are installed.
6.analogy: A local user account is like a key to one locker: it opens that locker and nothing else in the building, while a base-wide pass would open doors anywhere.
6.scenario: A squadron buys specialized training software with a single non-network license: it may be installed on one computer and cannot be shared over the network. The software goes on a computer set up with local user accounts, so the airmen of the section use it on that machine and the license agreement is not violated.
6.example: A shared kiosk in a lobby has its own sign-in that works only on that kiosk. In the course: Local user accounts allow the user to log into a specific machine and allow them to access resources on that machine only, Block Text p.69.

6.summary: A domain user account is stored in a central database on the domain controller and is valid on any computer in the domain, so the user can log on from any computer within the domain.
6.deeper:
Domain user account information is replicated to all domain controllers in a domain using directory replication. This replication enables the user to log on from any part of the domain quickly and easily. A domain user account is valid on any computer in the domain for which it was created, and it gives the user access to the different resources on the network that the user is given rights to.

All domain accounts are stored in a central database on the domain controller for that domain. This gives the administrator a central point to control who gets on the network and what resources they can access. If users need access to the network, they get domain user accounts; a local user account works on one machine only. Creating local and domain accounts is very similar, though local accounts have fewer options, and a system administrator mainly creates domain accounts.
6.analogy: A domain user account is like a base-wide access card kept on one central list and copied to every gate: the holder can enter at any gate, not just the one where the card was issued.
6.scenario: An administrator creates a domain user account for an airman. The account is stored in the central database on the domain controller and replicated to the other domain controllers in the domain. The next morning she logs on from a different computer in another building of the domain and still reaches the shared resources she is given rights to.

6.summary: Permissions control access to files, folders and directories; in Microsoft systems they are implemented with discretionary access control lists (DACLs) attached to the object they control.
6.deeper:
When you configure a folder on the shared drive so a specific user has read only access, you are configuring permissions: you are configuring that folder's ACL for that security object. The standard Windows permissions are Full Control, Modify, Read & execute, List folder contents, Read and Write.

Permissions can be controlled very extensively, and giving an untrained user control of the files on shared drives would be dangerous. So instead of letting the file creator assign permissions, shared drives are set up so that the Administrators are automatically placed in charge of all the files. File systems let new files inherit their parent directory's permissions: whenever a new file is created inside a folder, its permissions are assigned from the folder's permissions. Permissions differ from rights, which enable an account to perform predefined tasks.
6.analogy: Permissions are like the sign-out sheet on a filing cabinet drawer: the sheet stays on that drawer and lists who may only read the files and who may change them. A new file put in the drawer comes under the same sheet.
6.scenario: An airman sets a folder on the shared drive so that one user has read only access. He has just configured that folder's ACL. When a new file is later created inside the folder, it inherits the folder's permissions automatically.
6.example: A shared document can be set so some people may only view it and others may edit it, and the setting travels with that document. In the course: Permissions are implemented in Microsoft systems using discretionary access control lists (DACLs), which are attached to the object they control, Block Text p.70.

6.summary: Rights enable a user account or group to perform predefined tasks, from the basic right to log into a computer to advanced rights such as creating accounts and managing server functions.
6.deeper:
One of the most basic rights is the ability to log into a computer. More advanced rights can be given to grant authority to create accounts, change the date and time, and manage server functions. Rights are given to user or group accounts.

The management of rights is extremely important when setting up a network. Too many rights negatively impact the system: users can bring the network crashing to the ground, and giving an untrained, inexperienced user what amounts to an administrator account hands them a weapon that can bring the systems to their knees. Too few rights make users too restricted: they cannot access the resources they need, and may find all they can do after logon is stare at the desktop. Find an acceptable level of risk, as in a risk assessment: give users the ability to do the work their job requires.
6.analogy: Rights are like the keys handed to a new worker: too few and the worker stands outside locked doors all day; too many and an untrained hand can open the switch room and shut the power off.
6.scenario: A new airman joins a section, untrained and inexperienced. Instead of an administrator account, the airman gets the rights the job requires: logging into the computer and using the section's resources. A teammate who could only stare at the desktop after logon is given the missing rights, and nobody gets more than the work requires.
6.example: A new cashier gets a key to the register but not to the safe, which is enough to do the job without risking the store. In the course: Rights enable a user account or group to perform predefined tasks, Block Text p.71.

6.summary: Group Policy is a feature of the Microsoft Windows NT family of operating systems that controls the working environment of user accounts and computer accounts, with centralized management in Active Directory.
6.deeper:
Group Policy provides centralized management and configuration of operating systems, applications and user settings in an Active Directory environment. It enables policy-based administration using Microsoft Active Directory services, and it uses directory services and security group membership to provide flexibility and support extensive configuration information. Admins use it to tweak security protocols and practices, such as restricting Internet connection options, programs and even screen time.

Two kinds of settings are named. Policy settings are specified by an administrator. Group Policy preferences enable administrators to configure, deploy and manage greater numbers of operating system and application settings while still allowing the user to change their configuration. The settings are collected in Group Policy Objects (GPOs).
6.analogy: Group Policy is like a unit's standing orders issued from one office: everyone under them works the same way. Some orders are firm rules, others are default arrangements a person may still adjust at their own desk.
6.scenario: MSgt Rush must restrict Internet connection options on every workstation of a section. Instead of visiting each machine, an administrator sets it once through Group Policy in Active Directory, as a policy setting. A default application setting is deployed as a Group Policy preference, so users can still change it later.
6.example: A school sets the bell schedule for every classroom from the main office, while each teacher may still arrange the desks. In the course: Group Policy is a feature of the Microsoft Windows NT family of operating systems that controls the working environment of user accounts and computer accounts, Block Text p.71.

6.summary: Group Policy Objects (GPOs) are collections of Group Policy settings that define what a system will look like and how it will behave for a defined group of users.
6.deeper:
Policy settings are specified by an administrator and collected in a GPO. GPOs can be associated with a single container or with numerous Active Directory containers, including sites, domains or OUs; the systems of that group of users then look and behave as the settings define. The Microsoft Management Console (MMC) allows users to create GPOs that define registry-based policies, security options, software installation and much more.

Admins can also use GPOs to tweak several security protocols and practices, such as restricting Internet connection options, programs and even screen time. GPOs work within an Active Directory environment and give admins one place to configure, deploy and manage settings for many systems.
6.analogy: A GPO is like a uniform standard written down once and pinned to a unit's board: every member of that unit dresses to it, and the same sheet can be pinned on several boards.
6.scenario: An administrator collects settings that restrict certain programs and limit screen time into one GPO. She associates the GPO with an OU in Active Directory, and the systems of the users in that OU then behave as the settings define.
6.example: A school writes one set of computer-lab rules and posts it in every lab of one wing, so each lab runs the same way. 6.summary: A Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) is a DISA-generated configuration standard of cybersecurity requirements for a specific product.
6.deeper:
STIGs are designed to correct a security vulnerability in hardware or software, so they fall under the realm of logical security. They enhance security for software, hardware, physical and logical architectures to further reduce vulnerabilities.

Scanning tools identify whether network components are in STIG compliance. If a component is not in compliance, a STIG viewer is used to open the STIG and generate a checklist, which is used to document the findings.
6.analogy: A STIG is like a manufacturer's safety checklist for one model of vehicle: an inspector checks each vehicle against it, and any item that fails is written up on the inspection sheet.
6.scenario: A scanning tool reports that one of a unit's servers is not in STIG compliance. An airman opens the STIG for that product in a STIG viewer, which generates a checklist, and documents the findings on it.
6.example: A building inspector compares a new kitchen with the code for that kind of kitchen and writes down each item that does not match. In the course: A STIG is a DISA generated configuration standard consisting of cybersecurity requirements for a specific product, Block Text p.76.

7.summary: Services are utility programs that run silently in the background to monitor and take care of certain subsystems, so the operating system runs properly.
7.deeper:
In Linux these programs are called daemons; in Windows they are called services. Both run in the background and are not interactive with the user: from the desktop, they have no controlling terminal of their own. If the computer is on, they continue to exist and operate whether or not any user is logged into the server. They monitor and take care of certain subsystems so the operating system runs properly: a printer daemon monitors and takes care of printing services, and a network daemon monitors and maintains network communications. Other Windows examples are the Prefetch and Superfetch Service, which speeds up operating system and application startup by caching frequently used files to RAM, and the Background Intelligent Transfer Service, which moves files between machines over idle bandwidth and plays a key role in delivering software updates from servers to clients. A Windows service must conform to the rules of the Service Control Manager (SCM), the component responsible for managing Windows services. Services can be observed under the Services tab of Windows Task Manager or in the Microsoft Management Console (MMC) Services snap-in.

Active Directory Service: Active Directory is a service Microsoft developed for Windows networks. It oversees centralized domain management and identity-related functions.

DNS Client Service: this service resolves domain names to IP addresses and locally caches this data.
7.analogy: Services are like a building's night crew. Nobody at a desk calls them or talks to them; they keep the heat, the lights and the locks working whether anyone is in the office or not.
7.scenario: An airman signs out of a Windows server at the end of the shift. The server stays on, so its services keep running in the background with no one logged in: the Active Directory Service keeps overseeing domain management and identities, and the DNS Client Service keeps resolving domain names to IP addresses and caching the results. In the morning the airman opens the Services tab of Windows Task Manager to see what is running.
7.example: A refrigerator's thermostat keeps checking the temperature and switching the cooling on and off, with no one standing at the door to ask it. In the course: services are utility programs that run silently in the background to monitor and take care of certain subsystems to ensure that the operating system runs properly, Block Text p.78.

7.summary: Windows Task Manager is a handy utility that gives you a bird's-eye view of what's going on with your system; its Services tab lists the services running.
7.deeper:
Windows administrators can manage services through Windows Task Manager or through the Services snap-in built upon the Microsoft Management Console (MMC). Task Manager gives a bird's-eye view of the whole system and consists of seven tabs, one of them Services. The MMC hosts administrative tools used to maintain networks, computers, services and other system components, and the Services snap-in is one of those tools.

Services Tab: the Services tab of Windows Task Manager shows you all the current Windows 10 services running. It tells you what's running and what's not, and lets you see areas of Windows you did not know were affecting your system.

MMC Services: like Windows Task Manager, the MMC Services snap-in shows you all the current Windows 10 services running. It also shows the status of the services.
7.analogy: Task Manager is like the dashboard of a car: one glance shows what the engine is doing. Its Services tab is one gauge on that dashboard. The MMC is more like the mechanic's toolbox, and its Services snap-in is one tool in the box that also shows the services and their status.
7.scenario: An airman wants a quick look at what is happening on a workstation, so the airman opens Windows Task Manager and moves to its Services tab to see which services are running and which are not. Later the airman opens the MMC, which hosts the administrative tools, and uses its Services snap-in, which also shows the status of each service.
7.example: A shop's front window lets anyone passing see at a glance which machines inside are running. In the course: the Windows Task Manager is a handy utility that gives you a bird's-eye view of what's going on with your system, Block Text p.80.

8.summary: A process is the action happening when something is occurring on a computer: click the Yahoo application, and the process is Yahoo.exe, the executing file.
8.deeper:
A process is what runs when something is being done: when you click on the application Yahoo, the process is Yahoo.exe, the executing file. Processes can be located in Windows Task Manager on the Processes tab. However, some processes should never be deleted, because if they are terminated they can freeze or crash your system.

Processes Tab: the Processes tab in Task Manager breaks down how everything on your system is currently performing, giving insight into how system resources are being used. It is a great way to see if a program or service is causing issues with your PC. A value in the Processes tab gives you the option to end tasks, create dump files for troubleshooting, and learn more information about each process.

System (Ntoskrnl.exe): System (ntoskrnl.exe) is one of the processes that should never be deleted, along with others such as the Windows Logon Application (winlogon.exe) and the Windows Session Manager (smss.exe). Terminating it can freeze or crash the system.
8.analogy: Processes are like the machines running on a factory floor; the Processes tab is the supervisor's board that shows how hard each machine is working. Some machines can be switched off, but a few, like System (ntoskrnl.exe), must never be switched off, because stopping them can freeze or crash the whole floor.
8.scenario: An airman thinks a program may be causing issues with a PC. The airman checks the Processes tab, which shows how each program is using system resources, to see which program it is. The list also shows System (ntoskrnl.exe); the airman leaves it alone, because ending it can freeze or crash the system. To learn more about a program, the airman creates a dump file for troubleshooting.
8.example: When you switch on a blender, the spinning is what is happening right now; the blender sitting on the shelf is just the appliance. In the course: a process is the action happening when something is occurring, Block Text p.84.

8.summary: The Command shell (Command Prompt) was the first shell built into Windows to automate routine tasks, such as nightly backups, with batch (.bat) files.
8.deeper: Windows has two command-line shells: the Command shell (Command Prompt) and PowerShell. Each shell is a software program that provides direct communication between you and the operating system or application, giving an environment to automate IT operations. The Command shell came first and automates routine tasks, like user account management or nightly backups, with batch (.bat) files. With Windows Script Host, you could run more sophisticated scripts in the Command shell. Scripts accept all commands that are available at the command line, and you can perform operations more efficiently with scripts than with the user interface. The Command shell can only run Windows Commands, not PowerShell cmdlets; PowerShell was designed to extend its capabilities.
8.analogy: A batch file is like a written checklist handed to a helper: instead of doing each step yourself every night, you write the steps once and the helper runs through them. Windows Script Host is a stronger helper for longer, more involved checklists.
8.scenario: An airman is told to run the same backup every night. Doing it by hand through the user interface takes time, so the airman writes the steps into a batch (.bat) file and runs it in the Command shell. When the job needs a more sophisticated script, the airman runs it with Windows Script Host. When it needs PowerShell cmdlets, the Command shell cannot run them, so the airman moves to PowerShell.
8.example: A coffee maker with a timer starts the same brew every morning without anyone pressing the button. 8.summary: PowerShell is a Windows command-line shell that extends the Command shell: it runs commands called cmdlets as well as Windows Commands.
8.deeper: Windows has two command-line shells, the Command shell (Command Prompt) and PowerShell; each provides direct communication between you and the operating system or application. 8.summary: A server process is a task performed on a server, typically started automatically; its two types are work processes and communication processes.
8.deeper:
A server process is a task that is performed on a server. Server processes are typically initiated as automated processes on the server; the process might or might not be influenced by a server option or other setting, and it can also be started by a command. There are two types of server processes: work processes and communication processes. All server processes communicate with each other, and if one process fails, the remaining ones assume its queued tasks.

Work Process: a work process does the actual server work. Work processes activate, generate and execute tasks, and monitor them until they are finished. The one that starts first at system startup becomes the primary work process.

Communication Process: a communication process holds the connections to the agents and the user interfaces. All communication between agents and user interfaces is exclusively performed through the communication processes. After startup, a connection is established to the primary work process.
8.analogy: A server's processes are like a restaurant: the cooks are the work processes, making each order and watching it until it is done, and the servers on the floor are the communication processes, carrying every message between the guests and the kitchen.
8.scenario: An airman watches a server start. Its server processes come up automatically, with no command typed. A user interface sends a request; it passes through a communication process, which is connected to the primary work process. A work process activates and executes the task and monitors it until it is finished.
8.example: In a mailroom, sorters handle the letters while one clerk at the window talks to every visitor. In the course: a server process is a task that is performed on a server, Block Text p.85.

8.summary: The primary work process is the work process that starts first at system startup; it performs the central tasks that must not be allocated, such as the time basis.
8.deeper: Work processes do the actual server work: they activate, generate and execute tasks, and monitor them until they are finished. One of them has a special role. The primary work process performs central work-process tasks which must not be allocated, such as the time basis and process administration. It is chosen by timing: at system startup, the work process which starts first becomes the primary work process. If the primary work process fails, one of the remaining work processes assumes its task and becomes the primary work process. All relevant information is either regularly updated for all work processes or stored in the database. After startup, the communication processes also establish a connection to the primary work process.
8.analogy: The primary work process is like the first crew member to arrive on shift, who takes the keys and runs the shift log while the others do the regular work. If that person has to leave, another crew member picks up the keys and the log.
8.scenario: A server starts up and three work processes come up; the one that starts first becomes the primary work process and takes the time basis and process administration. Later the primary work process fails. One of the two remaining work processes assumes its task and becomes the new primary work process, and the server keeps working.
8.example: In a relay, the runner holding the baton carries it; if that runner drops out, a teammate takes the baton and the race goes on. In the course: at system startup, the work process which starts first becomes the primary work process, Block Text p.85.
